how: Calls propose a shared character, urge immediate participation and redirect later arrivals to the existing main effort.
The member proposing the main character also supplies its starting coordinates and attracts explicit contributions.
The starter's proposal already performs the call, so starting and calling are not separately observable chronological stages.
Replies to the main call commit to named pixels and continued participation, grounding a local call-to-building link.
The initial proposal receives a coordinates request and an invasion suggestion, so the later successful effort cannot retrospectively prove that this call produced building.
Representation remains open through compact lettering and proposals for stars, a companion and a separate number, without establishing that every proposal was built.
Members supply a starting location and undertake particular parts of the image, while the organiser later reports completion.
Members request coordinates, post the starting location and insist that placers follow a shared template.
A template instruction is visible, but the concepts do not show a design debate resolved by posting it.
One room's practical direction and chat invitations cannot test the aggregate prevalence claim or establish whether formal canvas authority was decided elsewhere.
The cited concepts preserve coordinates and template instructions but do not document machine operation, despite the blind account mentioning a bot target.
Defense and template use do not establish that pressure caused a turn to scripts or spare accounts.
A member gives a one-line promise to help maintain the character without requesting anything in return.
A direct reply accepts the main call by naming the pixels the member will work on, without requiring a bare assent formula.
One acceptance makes personal resource investment visible by reporting the purchase of in-flight connectivity to keep helping.
Completion becomes a defense instruction, followed by holding the line, maintenance commitments and an urgent dismantling warning.
The same organiser explicitly turns a reported completed image into a task of defending the work.
A neighbor distinguishes declared policy from placers removing a letter, giving a bounded account of apparent friendly interference.
Participants report limited helmet permission, request approval for surrounding black space and negotiate lettering around a neighboring border.
Part of the character occupies a neighbor's claimed box under permission limited to the helmet and excluding the host's text.
The organiser prohibits touching the host's remaining box, while visitors promise respect for borders and preservation of the room's lettering.
Reported permission supplies the precise boundary that the same instruction tells members to respect.
Permission and defense occur within one edited comment, so the record cannot establish that maintenance pressure initiated diplomacy.
A visitor explicitly claims responsibility for another project's diplomacy and opens a channel for contact.
Members ask to defend a smaller neighboring project and receive a neighboring community's explicit offer of protection.
Shared-fate language, mutual-defense proposals and invitations to both projects' chats show concrete commitments toward cooperation between rooms.
Chat invitations establish a route toward shared coordination, but actual attendance, settled decisions and durable coalition membership remain unresolved.
A request for a way to help receives invitations to both projects' chats, making the transfer into coordination venues observable.
The aid offer follows a defense warning as a separate reply, without establishing that the warning or a shortage of hands caused the offer.
Threat motivates an expressed wish to cooperate, but does not establish that a coalition was actually joined in response.
Border accommodation and help offers coexist, but no cited turn identifies a border bargain as the source of reciprocal assistance.
Failure to receive a policy memo does not explicitly dispute anyone's right to make an agreement for the room.
The visible compliance problem does not show border negotiation producing a dispute over who can bind placers.
A report that the character is gone does not by itself express a judgment that the room lacks enough hands or space.
Reported loss and a later final image do not identify a decision to relocate or a new building site.
The record does not connect the loss report to either an insufficiency judgment or a relocation decision.
Members use a familiar game character to represent the room and turn a visual flaw into recognizable character lore.
The proposed invasion names a canvas target without identifying any quarrel carried into the event.
The attack proposal supplies no prior tie or inherited rivalry as its reason.
Moderators require memes, suspend the ordinary rule and later restore it while rejecting a recurring meme day.
Members populate the takeover with game jokes, parody formats and deliberately unrelated material.
The licence operates through enforced rule reversal, invitations to return tomorrow and explicit compliance rather than only through interpretive uncertainty.
Participants maintain the shared joke by crediting makers, supplying sources, correcting formats and returning revised contributions.
Members circulate the joke through named communities and propose a one-day exchange without thereby establishing canvas alliances.
Ordinary game argument and help continue within the takeover, requiring an account of concurrent substantive practice rather than complete displacement by play.
A member turns a joke into a prospective prize challenge for a game feat, with neither completed canvas labour nor a recorded award.
A prospective reward for an in-game feat cannot instantiate celebration or reward of completed canvas work solely because both mention a prize.
The prank becomes a constraint in the room's recurring game challenge rather than a step in producing or preserving canvas art.
A canvas defense appeal receives a direct removal under the host's low-effort rule.
Selective removal of a canvas appeal does not establish that recruitment flooded the host or caused its separate meme-day rule changes.
The organiser announces completion and another post celebrates getting the character onto the canvas.
The same organiser marks the image as done within the organising record, and a later post celebrates that achieved character.
Celebrating an achieved image does not imply durable survival, because defense warnings and a loss report continue afterward.
A final-image title and discussion of neighboring pictures record a version of the work and its surroundings after placement stops.
A brief mourning turn records apparent loss without explaining its cause or duration.
Celebration precedes final-image discussion, but no cited turn says that marking the achievement caused its preservation.
A post-event wish for a different pixel does not establish contest over a cleaned shared archive or the event's historical account.
Members bring the finished canvas into the game, explain its origin and begin requesting a reusable flag file.
Explanation of the canvas appears inside post-event reuse, so sensemaking here follows participation rather than demonstrably generating the earlier critical mass.
The later reuse concerns the wider canvas, so its sequence after a final character image does not prove that this particular record caused the reuse.
A member proposes invading a colored corner in direct response to a request for the proposed character's location.
The recruiting thread gives rise to an invasion proposal, without demonstrating that the proposed attack was carried out.
The invasion suggestion receives an observation about the blue space, not a sustained contest with a named rival room.
The reply to the invasion suggestion does not refuse the attack or state a reason for restraint.
The invasion exchange contains no invocation of a truce or proposal to negotiate instead.
The invasion suggestion is not followed by coded taunts, victory claims or another turn carrying a rivalry forward.
